extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy; attendees of public lectures on pragmatism
extracted.subtask_description: A public-lecture-style exposition of the pragmatist conception of truth, arguing that truth is an event/process tied to verification and practical consequences rather than a static copying of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as verification
rubrics_metrics.description: TRUE IDEAS ARE THOSE THAT WE CAN ASSIMILATE, VALIDATE, CORROBORATE AND VERIFY. FALSE IDEAS ARE THOSE THAT WE CANNOT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James presents this as the central pragmatist thesis: truth is tied to the idea's capacity to be verified in experience. He contrasts this with intellectualist/copy theories of truth and treats verification as the touchstone for truth-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic 'cash-value' test
rubrics_metrics.description: "Grant an idea or belief to be true... what concrete difference will its being true make in anyone's actual life? ... what is the truth's cash-value in experiential terms?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ideas by asking what practical, experiential differences their truth would make (e.g., following a cow-path to a house to save oneself). The worth of a belief is judged by the concrete consequences it brings about in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a process/event (truth 'happens' to ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth of an idea is not a stagnant property inherent in it. Truth HAPPENS to an idea. It BECOMES true, is MADE true by events. Its verity is in fact an event, a process: the process namely of its verifying itself, its veri-FICATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess truth not as a static correspondence but as the unfolding process of validation through events and consequences; emphasize temporality and the dynamic nature of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification conceived as agreeable leading
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification/validation signify certain practical consequences... They lead us, namely, through the acts and other ideas which they instigate, into or up to, or towards, other parts of experience ... the connexions and transitions come to us from point to point as being progressive, harmonious, satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a belief, look for whether it reliably 'leads' us toward further satisfactory experiences or successful actions—this harmonious progression is what counts as verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness / instrumentality of true beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The possession of true thoughts means everywhere the possession of invaluable instruments of action; our duty to gain truth... can account for itself by excellent practical reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge theories by their utility as tools for action and problem-solving. Truths are often retained because they serve as instruments that produce desirable or reliable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect or circumstantial verification suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect as well as direct verifications pass muster. Where circumstantial evidence is sufficient, we can go without eye-witnessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that many everyday truths are verified indirectly (e.g., inferring that an object is a clock without seeing its works). Robust circumstantial support can be adequate for calling a belief true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple pragmatic tests of veracity (naturalness, intellectual economy, fruitfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their naturalness, their intellectual economy, their fruitfulness for practice, all start up as distinct tests of their veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate competing modes of thought (common sense, science, critical philosophy) on multiple pragmatic axes: how natural/intuitive they are, how economical (simple) the thinking is, and how fruitful they are in producing useful consequences. No single test is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories judged by use rather than literal copying
rubrics_metrics.description: According to these teachers no hypothesis is truer than any other in the sense of being a more literal copy of reality. They are all but ways of talking on our part, to be compared solely from the point of view of their USE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize evaluating theories by their heuristic and practical utility instead of by correspondence to an unknowable absolute reality; consider which theoretical language or model best serves intended uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense categories as historically discovered hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: OUR FUNDAMENTAL WAYS OF THINKING ABOUT THINGS ARE DISCOVERIES OF EXCEEDINGLY REMOTE ANCESTORS... they may have been successfully DISCOVERED by prehistoric geniuses ... and then from fact to fact and from man to man they may have SPREAD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat common-sense categories (thing, same/different, kinds, cause, time, space, self, etc.) as adaptive hypotheses validated by long survival and usefulness rather than as eternally given truths; assess their limits and domain of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief revision is gradual and integrative ('knowledge grows in spots')
rubrics_metrics.description: To begin with, our knowledge grows IN SPOTS... We patch and tinker more than we renew. The novelty soaks in; it stains the ancient mass; but it is also tinged by what absorbs it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing changes in belief or theory, expect gradual, localized modifications that integrate with existing beliefs rather than wholesale replacements; new ideas are typically assimilated and modified by prior beliefs.
